triplets.head: Impeachment process

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Subpoena witnesses and documents, conduct hearings, draft articles of impeachment, vote to report to full House

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Each article voted on separately by simple majority; only one article needs to pass for impeachment

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Members appointed as prosecutors in the Senate trial; historically from Judiciary Committee

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Sergeant at Arms commands silence; House manager reads articles aloud; presiding officer and senators sworn in

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: 'Do you solemnly swear that in all things appertaining to the trial of the impeachment... you will do impartial justice according to the Constitution and laws: So help you God'

triplets.head: Impeachment process

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Closed session (consistent practice since 1868); no member speaks more than once; 15 minutes max on final question

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: No uniform standard; Constitution does not specify; each Senator applies own standard in own conscience

triplets.head: Impeachment process
triplets.tail: Roll call on each article separately; senators vote 'guilty' or 'not guilty'; articles are not divisible

triplets.head: Impeachment process

triplets.head: Chief Justice role in impeachment

triplets.head: Chief Justice role in impeachment
triplets.tail: Any ruling can be overruled by a simple majority vote of Senators

triplets.head: Chief Justice role in impeachment
triplets.tail: If Senate splits 50-50, Chief Justice's provisional ruling stands; may cast a casting vote on procedural matters

triplets.head: Chief Justice role in impeachment

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: A term of art borrowed from 400+ years of English parliamentary practice, not ordinary criminal law terminology

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Modifies both 'crimes' and 'misdemeanors'; refers to offenses committed by persons in positions of special public authority who have taken an oath of office

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Impeachment of Michael de la Pole, Earl of Suffolk (1386) — for breaking promises to Parliament and failing to pay ransom

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Mason proposed 'maladministration'; Madison objected as too vague; Mason substituted 'other high Crimes and Misdemeanors' from English practice; adopted without further debate

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Offenses from 'the misconduct of public men, or the abuse or violation of some public trust' — 'POLITICAL, as they relate chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself'

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: 1) Exceeding/abusing constitutional powers; 2) Behavior grossly incompatible with office; 3) Using office for improper purposes or personal gain

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Criminality required — Benjamin Curtis, Robert Natelson (later work), Alan Dershowitz, Jonathan Turley

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Non-criminal misconduct sufficient — Raoul Berger, Charles Black, Michael Gerhardt, Noah Feldman, Cass Sunstein, Tribe & Matz, Bowman, 1974 Staff Report

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Breach of fiduciary duty — duties of loyalty, good faith, care, and accountability owed to the public (Natelson, earlier work)

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.relation: broad scholarly consensus on what it is NOT
triplets.tail: Not mere policy disagreements, not poor judgment or incompetence, not unpopularity, not 'whatever the House says'

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Congress — House decides what constitutes grounds; Senate decides whether to convict; Supreme Court has declined to review (Nixon v. United States, 1993)

triplets.head: 'High crimes and misdemeanors'
triplets.tail: Impeachment of Warren Hastings (Governor-General of India) for corruption and abuse of power was actively unfolding during the 1787 Convention; George Mason cited it specifically

triplets.head: Late impeachment debate
triplets.tail: Can a former president be tried by the Senate after leaving office?

triplets.head: Late impeachment debate

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Judge Walter L. Nixon Jr. challenged his Senate impeachment conviction, arguing Rule XI (committee hearing evidence) violated the Impeachment Trial Clause

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Nonjusticiable political question — courts cannot review how the Senate conducts impeachment trials

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Unanimous (9-0) in result; majority by Rehnquist, concurrences by White (with Blackmun) and Souter

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: The word 'sole' in 'sole Power to try' means authority is reposed in the Senate and nowhere else; appears only twice in the Constitution, both for impeachment

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: The word 'try' lacks sufficient precision to afford any judicially manageable standard of review

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Three specific requirements (oath, two-thirds vote, Chief Justice presides) suggest Framers did not intend additional limitations by use of word 'try'

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Judicial review would cause months or years of chaos, especially in presidential impeachment; difficulty of fashioning relief

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Powell involved specific constitutional qualifications for House membership that limited Congress; no analogous separate provision limits Senate's impeachment trial discretion

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Agreed case was nonjusticiable but on case-by-case basis; if Senate convicted 'upon a coin-toss' or 'a summary determination that an official was simply a bad guy,' judicial interference might be appropriate

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Believed case was justiciable but Senate wins on merits; Senate has 'very wide discretion'; intervention if Senate 'automatically entered judgment of conviction whenever articles delivered'

triplets.head: Nixon v. United States (1993)
triplets.tail: Revived political question doctrine; established Congress as constitutional interpreter in impeachment; framed all subsequent impeachment debates

triplets.head: Impeachment verdict finality
triplets.tail: An impeachment verdict — whether conviction or acquittal — is for all practical purposes absolutely final and unreviewable

triplets.head: Impeachment verdict finality
triplets.tail: Constitution does not grant Supreme Court original or appellate jurisdiction over impeachment; Convention delegates deliberately dropped 'impeachment' from Article III judicial power

triplets.head: Impeachment verdict finality
triplets.tail: Over 230 years of unbroken practice with no judicial review of any impeachment; no conviction ever successfully challenged

triplets.head: Impeachment verdict finality
triplets.tail: Courts might find justiciable a violation of explicit textual constraints: oath requirement, two-thirds vote, Chief Justice presiding, or penalty limited to removal/disqualification

triplets.head: Raoul Berger, Impeachment: The Constitutional Problems (1973)
triplets.tail: Founding text of modern impeachment scholarship; every subsequent work responds to it

triplets.head: Raoul Berger, Impeachment: The Constitutional Problems (1973)
triplets.tail: 'High crimes and misdemeanors' is a 'limited, technical' term of art; does not require an indictable crime; historically encompassed abuse of power, corruption, neglect of duty

triplets.head: Raoul Berger, Impeachment: The Constitutional Problems (1973)
triplets.tail: Exhaustive originalist analysis of English impeachment precedents from 1386 forward, Convention debates, and early American impeachments

triplets.head: Raoul Berger, Impeachment: The Constitutional Problems (1973)
triplets.tail: Standard should be applied more strictly to presidents than to judges — widely criticized as inconsistent with constitutional text

triplets.head: Raoul Berger, Impeachment: The Constitutional Problems (1973)
triplets.tail: Argued courts could review impeachment convictions — later rejected by Supreme Court in Nixon v. United States (1993)

triplets.head: Charles Black, Impeachment: A Handbook (1974; updated 2018 by Philip Bobbitt)
triplets.tail: 'The standard work' (Lawfare); 'the premier guide to presidential impeachment' (Yale University Press)

triplets.head: Charles Black, Impeachment: A Handbook (1974; updated 2018 by Philip Bobbitt)
triplets.tail: Impeachable offenses must involve 'a serious assault on the integrity of the processes of government' or conduct 'grossly incompatible with the office held and subversive of our constitutional system'

triplets.head: Charles Black, Impeachment: A Handbook (1974; updated 2018 by Philip Bobbitt)
triplets.tail: Structural/purposive constitutional reasoning using six modalities of argument: text, history, structure, doctrine, prudence, and ethos

triplets.head: Charles Black, Impeachment: A Handbook (1974; updated 2018 by Philip Bobbitt)
triplets.tail: Each senator should find own standard in own conscience; removal of a president should require 'overwhelming preponderance of the evidence'

triplets.head: Michael Gerhardt, The Federal Impeachment Process (1996; 3rd ed. 2019)

triplets.head: Michael Gerhardt, The Federal Impeachment Process (1996; 3rd ed. 2019)
triplets.tail: Impeachable offenses are 'political crimes, abuse of power, breaches of the public trust, and serious injuries to the Republic'; need not be criminal

triplets.head: Michael Gerhardt, The Federal Impeachment Process (1996; 3rd ed. 2019)
triplets.tail: Addresses severability of impeachment sanctions, precedential effect of prior impeachments, nonjusticiability, and whether Congress can make constitutional law through impeachment practice

triplets.head: Cass Sunstein, Impeachment: A Citizen's Guide (2017)
triplets.tail: Impeachable offenses involve abuse of presidential authority or serious violation of public trust; Framers borrowed phrase from English law with settled technical meaning

triplets.head: Cass Sunstein, Impeachment: A Citizen's Guide (2017)
triplets.tail: Most accessible of the major works — written for a general audience; systematically rebuts common misconceptions

triplets.head: Laurence Tribe & Joshua Matz, To End a Presidency (2018)

triplets.head: Laurence Tribe & Joshua Matz, To End a Presidency (2018)
triplets.tail: Most sustained treatment of political and strategic dimensions — not just what is impeachable but when impeachment is wise and dangers of normalization

triplets.head: Frank Bowman, High Crimes and Misdemeanors: A History of Impeachment for the Age of Trump (2019)

triplets.head: Frank Bowman, High Crimes and Misdemeanors: A History of Impeachment for the Age of Trump (2019)
triplets.tail: Most historically comprehensive single-volume treatment — 465 pages covering English precedents through Trump
